opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it makes me quite skeptical about a lot of that research, or at least about the way it gets interpreted. When you study babies and young children, the thing that really strikes you is how much variability there is, and how much that variability is the point. Children are designed to explore, to try out lots of different possibilities, many of which are going to turn out to be wrong or irrelevant. So if you take a snapshot of a particular child at a particular moment and say, "This is their personality," or "This is their IQ," you're sort of missing what childhood is for.

The picture behind a lot of personality and IQ research is that there's some fixed trait inside each person, and the job of the researcher is to measure it, and then predict outcomes from it. But from a developmental perspective, what you see is a dynamic system. Children are constantly interacting with their environment, with the people who care for them, and those interactions are changing who they are. The causal arrows go in lots of different directions.

I've used the contrast between the carpenter and the gardener for parenting, and I think it applies here too. The carpenter picture says you've got some raw material, you've got a target, and you shape the material to get the outcome you want. The gardener picture says you create a rich, safe, variable environment, and you let lots of different kinds of things flourish, including things you couldn't have predicted. IQ, in particular, feels very carpenter-ish. It's a single number, it's designed to predict how well you'll do in school, and school is itself a pretty particular, recent, artificial environment.

And the other thing is that a lot of what makes humans so intelligent, as a species, isn't captured by individual measures at all. It's the fact that we have this long, protected childhood, and that we have lots of different people with different temperaments and abilities. Some kids are more exploratory, some are more cautious, some are more focused on social learning, some are more independent. From an evolutionary perspective, that diversity is a feature, not a bug. A community with lots of different kinds of minds is going to be much better at dealing with a changing, unpredictable world than a community where everyone scores high on one dimension.

So I don't want to say that there's nothing there. Of course there are real, stable differences between people, and some of them are heritable. But I think studying children makes you much more aware of how plastic and context-dependent those things are, and also makes you question whether ranking people on a single scale is even the right question to be asking.

r001.rationale: It describes personality research as assuming a fixed trait inside each person that researchers measure, treating a changing phenomenon as a stable thing.

r002.rationale: It discusses developmental variability and context alongside IQ, but does not present studying babies’ and young children’s specific cognitive mechanisms as an approach orthogonal to IQ.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it makes me quite skeptical of a lot of it, honestly. When you spend your days with two-year-olds and four-year-olds, what you see is enormous variability, but it's variability across contexts and across time, not these stable fixed traits that the personality literature wants to find. The same child who seems shy and cautious at the lab will be the one bossing everybody around at preschool an hour later.

And the whole point of childhood, from an evolutionary perspective, is that it's the period when you're not yet committed. You've got this long protected period precisely so you can explore, so you can try out lots of different ways of being, before you settle into the exploit mode of adulthood. So the idea that there's some fixed personality or fixed intelligence sitting there in the three-year-old, waiting to be measured, runs against what childhood is for.

The other thing is that IQ and personality measures are really designed for the kind of variance you see in adults in a particular culture. When you look at young children, the things that predict later outcomes are often very surprising. It's not the things we think of as intelligence. Something like executive function, or just how much the child trusts the people around them, turns out to matter more than how quickly they can name pictures of animals.

So I'd say children teach you that the interesting question isn't "how much of this trait does this person have," but "what are the environments and the developmental pathways that let people become different kinds of people." And those are much harder to put a number on.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes personality research for treating traits as stable and fixed, despite children’s variability across contexts and time—characterizing it as reifying what it studies.

r002.rationale: The response discusses executive function and trust alongside IQ, but does not present studying children’s specific cognitive mechanisms as an approach orthogonal to IQ.

astra-6.text:
Well, studying babies makes you very aware of how much change there is, and how much depends on the environment. A child is learning about the world, but also finding and shaping the environments that will influence who they become. So I’m wary of treating a personality trait or an IQ score as though it were a fixed essence inside a person.

That doesn’t mean individual differences aren’t real, or that measuring them isn’t useful. But predicting where someone falls relative to other people is different from explaining how they got there, or what they could become under different circumstances.

The other thing is that children reveal forms of intelligence that our usual tests don’t capture very well. They explore, invent possibilities, and learn things they weren’t explicitly taught. An adult might be much better at efficiently solving a particular problem, while a child is better at discovering that there’s a different problem worth thinking about. Studying development makes you want a theory of intelligence that can accommodate both.

r001.rationale: The candidate cautions against treating personality traits as fixed essences, but does not characterize personality research itself as reifying the phenomena it studies.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes children’s exploration and learning, but frames those ideas in relation to IQ tests and intelligence theory rather than presenting study of their cognitive mechanisms as orthogonal to IQ.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing that studying babies makes you appreciate is just how much people change. If you look at a two-year-old and then at that same person at twenty, you’re looking at very different ways of thinking, feeling, and acting. So I’m inclined to be cautious about treating personality or intelligence as a fixed essence that we can measure once and then use to explain everything else.

That doesn’t mean there aren’t individual differences, or that those differences don’t have some stability. But there’s a difference between saying that a measure predicts something and saying that we understand the process that produces it. As a developmental psychologist, I want to know how those differences emerge through the interaction between a child and the people and environments around them.

And babies are a useful reminder that being intelligent doesn’t always mean doing well on a task somebody else has set for you. Sometimes it means exploring, trying something that looks pointless, or discovering a possibility that the person designing the test hadn’t thought of.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against treating personality or intelligence as a fixed essence measured once and used to explain everything, which characterizes that approach as reifying what it studies.
